item.text: {"question_id":"3B.7","answer":"During 2023, the government maintained and added formal protection measures, but the supplied evidence does not establish effective, adequately funded, or equitable nationwide protection for vulnerable groups. The December 2022 Indigenous-peoples law and conflict-related sexual-violence framework were inherited statutory measures in force during the period, while a September 2023 order-act criminalized gender-based violence; the government also reported inquiries, police stations, community policing, patrols near IDP camps, multisectoral survivor centres, mobile clinics, legal clinics, safe spaces, counselling, and a reparations fund (BATCH-0001-E010; BATCH-0029-E002; BATCH-0011-E003; BATCH-0011-E006). These establish formal acts and reported service activity, but the government submission does not independently verify implementation, enforcement, equitable access, or completed remedies. UNFPA programme data likewise show that government implementation represented only 4% of GBV spending, 3% of gender-and-social-norms spending, 3% of quality-of-care spending, and 14% of maternal-death-reduction spending; the data do not establish presidential direction or outcome attainment (BATCH-0029-E006). Some services produced concrete, partner-supported outputs: UNFPA-supported facilities enabled more than 31,000 safe deliveries at over 24 facilities, and mobile clinics served displaced populations, but these outputs cannot be attributed as Tshisekedi-directed national results (BATCH-0025-E003). Exposure and access failures remained severe. In eastern DRC, approximately 220,000 women were pregnant amid fragile infrastructure and exceptionally difficult access to maternal and newborn care; sexual violence increased, displaced women and girls faced heightened rape risks and limited medical, psychosocial, legal, and socioeconomic support, and late-2023 fighting displaced more than 450,000 people in North Kivu, bringing national displacement to 6.9 million, with remote areas receiving little or no assistance (BATCH-0008-E002; BATCH-0008-E003; BATCH-0013-E014). Children faced comparable protection failures: more than 800,000 were displaced during 2023 and over 2,000 schools closed in eastern provinces because of insecurity and displacement, while children were more exposed to abuse, child labor, and child marriage (BATCH-0022-E010). Broader reporting also described persistent discrimination, widespread sexual and gender-based violence, rare convictions, forced labor, and child recruitment by government forces and armed groups, though the source does not isolate Tshisekedi’s personal responsibility or fully distinguish state from non-state perpetrators (BATCH-0002-E022). Amnesty documented forced evictions, beatings, sexual assault, and ineffective grievance mechanisms involving companies and state authorities, but much of the conduct predated 2023 and personal presidential direction was not established (BATCH-0010-E018). Overall, the target-period evidence supports enacted and partly organized protection with limited demonstrated reach, uneven regional access, severe recurring or widespread vulnerability, and weakly verified enforcement and remedy; it does not establish systematic state terror or prove that all adverse conditions were personally caused by
